FEZ

Personal Sound Computer
a forth programmable virtual analog synth engine

01First sound

FEZ is a synthesiser you program. One voice makes the sound; a few lines of a small language, kept in blocks, decide what the voice does and when. You write a line such as C4 PITCH !, press a key, and the note changes. This chapter takes you from switching on to a sound you made yourself.

Start it

On a computer you need a C compiler and the SDL2 library (which draws the window and plays the sound). From the project folder:

make fez
./fez

On the TrimUI Brick, copy the FEZ folder onto the card and start it from the Tools menu; the handheld chapter has the details. The rest of this chapter uses the desktop keys. The Brick's buttons do the same jobs.

The window is cut into three tiles: the editor on the left, a scope (a picture of the sound wave) at top right, and the CTRL list below it. Ctrl+Tab changes the layout, and F1 shows every key on one page. The app starts from a blank patch, which is silent until something plays it.

Load something that plays itself

  1. Press Ctrl+] to move to the PATCHES tab.
  2. Press Right to switch from MY PATCHES to EXAMPLES. The thirteen built-in patches are listed. Typing letters narrows the list.
  3. Pick one with Up and Down and press Enter.

Glass Bells is a good first choice: it plays random bells by itself, using the pulsers (small clocks that start blocks of code, explained in Control). If you hear nothing, press Ctrl+P in case the pulsers are off. The sound is stopped at once with Shift+Esc (mute), which fades the output in 20 milliseconds and leaves everything running.

Play one note

Press Ctrl+G. That fires the gate, which is the on-switch of a note: it opens the envelope (the rise and fall of loudness) once. Press it again and the note repeats. A synthesiser with no keyboard still needs something to say "now", and the gate is that.

Change a number

  1. Press Ctrl+] until you reach CTRL, the list of every register. A register is a named number that the sound reads. CUTOFF is how open the filter is, PITCH is the note, and so on.
  2. Pick CUTOFF with Up and Down.
  3. Press Left and Right to change it (hold Shift for bigger steps), or type a number and press Enter.
  4. Press Ctrl+G after each change and listen.

Nothing here is special to the screen. A register is the same thing whether a person turns it or a line of code writes it. That is how the whole instrument works.

Write a line

Go back to the EDITOR tab (Ctrl+[). The editor holds sixteen blocks; [ and ] move between them. Pick an empty one, and type:

C4 PITCH !
1 GATE !

Read it aloud as "C4, into PITCH; 1, into GATE". The first line sets the note, and the second opens the gate. The ! means "store this number in that register". The next chapter explains why the order is value first, register second.

Typing changes nothing yet. This is deliberate: a half-typed line never alters the sound. Press Ctrl+Enter to apply the block (the editor compiles it and swaps it in), or Ctrl+R to apply it and run it once. Press Ctrl+R: you should hear a C. Change C4 to E4, press Ctrl+R again, and the note moves up four semitones.

If the block has a mistake, the editor says what and where, in red, and keeps the old version running. Try typing -5: it refuses with no negative numbers: write 5 NEG. The language chapter explains why.

Keep it

Press Ctrl+S, type a name, and press Enter. The patch is saved as a plain text file in ~/FEZ/patches/, and appears under MY PATCHES. There is no autosave: a patch you do not save is gone when you quit. Press Ctrl+T to record what you hear to a WAV file in ~/FEZ/recordings/, and Ctrl+T again to stop.

Where to go next

  • For a picture of how the parts fit together, read the overview.
  • To understand the lines you have just typed, read the language.
  • To see what the other registers do, read the voice.

02How it fits together

FEZ is two machines joined by a set of numbers. One makes sound. The other decides, every five milliseconds, what the sound should do next. The numbers they share are called registers.

The sound path

Three sources feed the mixer: a complex oscillator (a sine blended with a second wave, then bent by the wavefolder), a mod oscillator and noise. The mixer's sum goes through the lowpass gate. The gate does two jobs with one control: it sets how loud a note is and how bright. A note that fades also dulls, which is why FEZ sounds struck rather than switched.

The mod voice is a second path, built for slow sweeps. It takes the same mod oscillator and the same noise as the mixer does, and runs them through a ladder filter of its own. The buffer device records one of four things, as the register BWSRC chooses: the mixer's sum, the voice, the mod voice, or both voices together. It plays the recording back either into the mixer or straight on to the effects.

The three paths are then added together, and from here on everything is treated alike. First comes the tape delay, then the spring, then the compressor. Until the spring the signal is a single channel. The spring's two tanks give each ear its own reverb, so the sound turns stereo there and stays so. The compressor has no controls. It holds the level down when the loops build up, so that a delay at full feedback cannot overload the output.

The control path

Nothing in FEZ happens by itself except time. Four pulsers keep it, firing as often as you set, in pulses a minute. When a pulser fires, each block that listens to it runs once.

A block is a short program in FEZ's own language. It can read any register and write most of them: change a pitch, open a filter, fire another pulser, leave a number for another block to find. Between runs a block remembers only what is in the registers (and, after YIELD, where it stopped), which is why the registers sit at the centre of the picture.

Devices add numbers that nobody typed. The cellular automaton, the Lorenz attractor, the sequencer, the Turing machine and the keyboard each write their results into registers. Some fire pulsers (the automaton, the attractor, the keyboard). Others are stepped by them (the sequencer, the Turing machine, the grains of the buffer). A pattern in one device can therefore become notes in another.

The matrix lies between the registers and the sound. Each route takes a source, multiplies it by a weight and adds the result to a register's value. The sound reads that sum, not the number you wrote.

A register holds what you wrote. What you hear is that value plus whatever the matrix adds. If a knob seems to have no effect, check the matrix: a route may be adding an opposite amount.

03The language

The language is small: 46 words, a stack and some registers. It is a cousin of Forth, an old language built on a stack. You do not need to know Forth. Everything here is explained from nothing, and the whole language fits on one page of the word reference at the end of the manual.

The stack

Think of a pile of cards. A number you write goes on top of the pile. A word that needs numbers takes them from the top, and puts its answer back on the pile. That pile is the stack, and it replaces the brackets and variables you may know from other languages.

2 3 +

Read left to right. 2 goes on the stack, then 3 goes on top of it, and + takes both and leaves 5. There are no brackets because the order does the work: to compute (2 + 3) minus 1, you write 2 3 + 1 -.

The stack holds 16 numbers. Taking from an empty stack, or putting a seventeenth on a full one, is a fault (see below).

Stack pictures

Every word in the reference has a picture of what it does to the stack, such as ( a b -- c ). Everything left of the two dashes is what the word takes, and everything on the right is what it leaves. The top of the stack is on the right. So - is ( a b -- a-b ): it takes b from the top, a from beneath it, and leaves a minus b. 10 3 - leaves 7.

Four words move numbers about without changing them. DUP copies the top, DROP throws it away, SWAP trades the top two, and OVER copies the second to the top. ROT brings the third to the top: after 1 2 3 ROT the stack holds 2, 3, 1 (top).

Numbers

A number can be written four ways, and each is one token:

12000       \ a whole number, 0 to 32767
0x2A54      \ the same sort of number in hexadecimal (base 16)
.5          \ a fraction of full scale: .5 is 16384, half of 32768
A4          \ a note name: C-1 to G9; # sharp, b flat

A fraction is a number between 0 and 1 written with a point. It is stored as that fraction of 32768, so .25 is 8192 and .99 is 32440. Fractions are the natural way to write a register that runs from nothing to full, such as a filter cutoff. A note name is stored as a pitch; see Pitch for what that number means. A note name always includes its octave: C4 is middle C.

Tokens and slots

A program is a row of tokens separated by spaces: a number, a note name, a register name or a word. Each token takes exactly one slot, which is one place in the block's memory. A block has 128 slots and a word has 24, and the editor shows how many you have used. There is no trick in the counting: five tokens are five slots.

That has a consequence for numbers. A number has no sign. To write -5 you write 5 NEG: the number, then the word that changes its sign. That is two tokens and two slots, and you can see both. If you type -5 the editor says no negative numbers: write 5 NEG and refuses to run the block.

5 NEG        \ -5
.5 NEG       \ minus a half
12 ST NEG    \ twelve semitones down: an octave below

The rule is kept this strict on purpose, so that SKIP, which jumps over the next slot, always jumps over exactly the next token you can see.

Numbers stop at the ends

Every number in FEZ is a whole number from -32768 to 32767, the range that fits in 16 binary digits (the "16 bit" you will see in the source). Most programming languages let a number that runs past one end wrap round to the other: add 1 to 32767 and you get -32768. FEZ does not. A result that goes past either end sticks there. The usual word for this is saturating: the number is full and takes no more.

30000 5000 +        \ 32767, not 35000
30000 NEG 5000 -    \ -32768, not -35000
32767 NEG 1 -       \ -32768
32767 NEG 1 - NEG   \ 32767: -32768 has no positive twin

Sticking is the right behaviour for sound. A cutoff pushed past fully open should stay open. If it wrapped, it would jump to fully shut, and you would hear a crack.

The check happens at every step, not at the end, so the order of a sum matters. 30000 5000 + 5000 - leaves 27767, because the first sum was cut to 32767 before 5000 was taken off. Take away first and add after, 30000 5000 - 5000 +, and you get 30000. The word */, which multiplies and then divides, keeps the full product between its two steps, so 20000 20000 20000 */ correctly leaves 20000.

The words that stop at the ends are +, -, *, /, */, NEG, ABS and SHL. The bit words (AND, OR, XOR, NOT, SHR, ROL and ROR) work on the 16 binary digits as they are and never stick: 1 NEG 4 SHR leaves 4095, because the digits move right and zeros come in at the top. Words that only compare or choose (MIN, MAX, =, <, >) cannot overflow.

Registers stop at their own ends too. Most hold 0 to 32767, so 5 NEG CUTOFF ! leaves the cutoff at 0 and 30000 5000 + CUTOFF ! leaves it at 32767. The registers meant for signed numbers (CV0 to CV3 and the scratch slots S0 to S15) hold -32768 to 32767.

A number you type is limited as well. The largest is 32767, and a larger one is an error when you apply the block (literal out of range), not a silent cut. The most negative number, -32768, cannot be typed at all: write 32767 NEG 1 -.

Two kinds of multiply

* multiplies whole numbers, as + and - add and subtract them: 6 7 * leaves 42. Sound, however, is mostly proportions: half as loud, a quarter as bright. For that there is F*, the fraction multiply, in which 32768 stands for 1.0. So .5 .5 F* leaves .25 (8192), and 20000 .5 F* leaves 10000: half of 20000. Use F* to scale a register by a proportion, and * for counting. Mixing them up is easy to spot: 6 7 F* leaves 0, because six thirty-two-thousandths of seven thirty-two-thousandths is too small to count.

To multiply and then divide by a whole number, use */: 100 3 4 */ leaves 75. It keeps the full product between its two steps, so a big intermediate number does not stick.

Registers

A register is a named number that something else reads. The voice reads CUTOFF and PITCH; the delay reads DLYTIME. Each has an address, a small whole number, and the name is only a nickname for it. So when you write CUTOFF, what goes on the stack is the address.

  • @ reads: ( address -- value ). CUTOFF @ leaves the cutoff on the stack.
  • ! writes: ( value address -- ). 12000 CUTOFF ! stores 12000 there.

The value goes first because it must already be on the stack when the address arrives. Registers keep their own limits. Most hold 0 to 32767, and a few are read-only, such as KBGATE; writing to one is a fault.

To add one to a register, read it, add, and write it back:

CUTOFF @ 100 + CUTOFF !

Scratch registers and private ones

You will often want somewhere to keep a number between ticks. There are two places. S0 to S15 are sixteen scratch registers that every block can see, so blocks can leave each other messages. P0 to P15 are private: each block has its own, and no other block can touch them. Use P for a counter that belongs to one block, and S to share. Both hold -32768 to 32767.

P0 @ 1 + P0 !     \ count how many times this block has run

Blocks, words and ticks

Code lives in blocks. There are sixteen, each up to 128 slots long. A block does nothing until something runs it: a pulser, the sequencer, a key press, or another block. When it runs it goes once from top to bottom and stops. It does not loop on its own.

A word is a short program kept apart from the blocks, 24 slots at most, that any block can run with W. 3 W runs word 3. Words share the stack with whoever calls them, so a word can take its inputs and leave its answer there, like a built-in. There are sixteen.

FEZ works in steps called ticks. One tick is five milliseconds, so there are 200 a second. In each tick the pulsers that are due fire, the blocks they started run, and the registers settle on their new values for the sound to read. A block can therefore change anything it likes, as often as it likes, and what you hear is the state at the end of each tick. Blocks run between stretches of sound, never during one, so a block cannot make the sound glitch by running late.

A block also has a safety limit of 256 steps per run. A loop that never ends stops there and is reported as a fault, instead of freezing the instrument.

When something goes wrong

A fault is a mistake caught while a block runs. Some stop the block: taking from an empty stack, a jump to a label that is not there, a loop that reaches the step limit. The block halts, and the editor shows HALTED in red with one line on what went wrong, such as ! needs 2, stack had 1, and marks the word that caused it with a red block. If the fault happened inside a word you defined, the line starts in a word: and the mark is on the W that called it. Others let the block run on, because a sensible answer exists: dividing by zero gives 0, and writing to a register that cannot be written does nothing. These show the same kind of line in amber, such as ! to KBGATE: cannot be written. The rest of FEZ carries on either way. Press Ctrl+Enter to apply the block again, which clears the fault and restarts it.

Division by zero is the one gentle fault. 1 0 / leaves 0, notes the fault, and the block carries on.

Making decisions and loops

A label is a name for a place in a block. 3 L marks the place as label 3 (there are 16, numbered 0 to 15). 3 JMP jumps to it. JZ jumps if a number is zero, and JNZ jumps if it is not:

0 S0 !                 \ start the count at 0
1 L                    \ label 1: the top of the loop
S0 @ 1 + S0 !          \ add one
S0 @ 4 < 1 JNZ         \ if S0 is below 4, go back to label 1

The comparison 4 < leaves 1 for true or 0 for false, which is the flag that JNZ tests. After this runs, S0 holds 4.

For the commonest small decision there is ?, which picks one of two numbers: ( a b flag -- a or b ) leaves b if the flag is not zero and a if it is. And SKIP takes a flag and, if it is 0, skips the very next token.

For chance there is P, ( percent -- flag ): it leaves 1 that many times in a hundred and 0 otherwise, so 50 P is a coin toss. With ? it makes a melody that mostly stays put and sometimes leaps:

C4 G4 30 P ? PITCH !   \ C4, but G4 three times in ten
1 GATE !

Two words stop a block early or in pieces. EXIT stops it for now. YIELD stops it and, the next time the block runs, carries on from that point, not from the top. That makes a step-by-step block simple to write:

S0 @ 1 + S0 !          \ first run: add one, then pause
YIELD
S0 @ 10 + S0 !         \ second run: add ten, then start again

Rotating a pattern

A number is also a row of 16 on-or-off bits, and a row of bits is a pattern: which steps of a rhythm sound, which cells of the automaton are alive. ROL and ROR slide such a pattern round like a ring. The bits that fall off one end come back in at the other, so none are lost. SHL and SHR cannot do this: SHL is a multiplication that sticks at the top (see Numbers stop at the ends), and both fill with zeros.

Here is a complete rhythm. The pattern is 16 steps, one bit each: a 1 plays a note and a 0 is a rest. Run this once to set it:

0x1249 S0 !          \ the pattern: a note every third step

Then give a block to a pulser. Each time it runs it looks at the bottom bit, plays if it is set, and turns the pattern one place so the next bit comes round:

S0 @ 1 AND 1 JZ      \ bottom bit 0? stay silent
1 GATE !             \ bottom bit 1: play a note
1 L
S0 @ 1 ROR S0 !      \ turn the pattern one place right

After 16 runs the pattern is back where it began. Change a bit of S0 while it plays and the rhythm changes at once. ROL turns the pattern the other way. The same trick works on the automaton's row: CAROW @ 3 ROR CAROW ! turns it three cells round.

Pitch

In FEZ a pitch is an ordinary whole number. One semitone, the step between two neighbouring piano keys, is 256. An octave is twelve semitones, so it is 3072.

The rule for turning a note into a number is to take its MIDI note number and multiply by 256. Middle C is MIDI note 60, so it is 60 × 256 = 15360. The A above it, the note orchestras tune to, is note 69, so it is 17664. The register PITCH holds this number.

Numbers that fall between the whole semitones are the notes between the keys. 128 more than a note is a quarter-tone sharp of it. One unit is about four-tenths of a cent, and a cent is a hundredth of a semitone, finer than anyone can hear.

Programmers call this 8.8 fixed point, and you will see the phrase in the source code. It means that the 16-bit number is split in two: the top eight bits count whole semitones and the bottom eight count 256ths of one. You never need to think in bits. "Multiply by 256" is the whole rule. The reason for doing it this way is that whole numbers give the same answer on every computer, including the small one inside the TrimUI Brick, with no rounding surprises. The same trick, with a different split, is behind the fractions such as .5.

There are three ways to write a pitch. They give the same kind of number, so you can mix them:

C4          \ a note name: 15360
60 ST       \ 60 semitones: 15360 again
4400 HZ     \ 440 Hz in tenths of a hertz: 17664, the A

To transpose, add. ST turns a number of semitones into the right amount to add, so a fifth up is seven semitones:

PITCH @ 7 ST + PITCH !      \ add a fifth to the pitch

To go down, make the amount negative: 12 ST NEG is an octave below. Registers hold 0 to 32767, so the top of the range is note 127 (G9).

The word COLOUR works on the same scale: it gives the distance above a root note, and you add the root yourself.

04The voice

FEZ has two sound sources, and they are not alike. The voice plays notes: it is gated, so it is silent until a note starts, and it fades after. The mod voice is always running, and does the slow, steady work of drones, noise and sweeps. Both feed the effects described in Space. Both are set by registers, so the editor, the CTRL list, a block and the matrix can all reach every knob below.

How the knobs are scaled

Every register holds 0 to 32767, but the things it controls are not that. A cutoff is a frequency, an attack is a time. FEZ spreads the 32768 steps exponentially, which is how ears hear: each equal step multiplies the frequency or the time by the same factor, instead of adding the same amount. So the bottom half of a cutoff knob is spent between 40 Hz and about 750 Hz, and the top half between 750 Hz and 14 kHz. Here is where five settings land:

register value08192163842457632767
CUTOFF, MDCUT40 Hz173 Hz748 Hz3.2 kHz14.0 kHz
ATK1 ms10 ms100 ms1.0 s10 s
REL10 ms45 ms200 ms895 ms4.0 s
LFORATE0.05 Hz0.22 Hz1.00 Hz4.47 Hz20 Hz
NZTONE100 Hz376 Hz1.4 kHz5.3 kHz20.0 kHz
FMAMT (depth)0 Hz125 Hz500 Hz1125 Hz2000 Hz

The CTRL tab shows the real value next to the number, so you rarely need this table. It explains one thing, though: patches with slow notes need values above 25000. A release of 12000 lasts only about 0.1 seconds, and one of 28000 about 1.7 seconds.

The voice

The voice has four stages in a row: an oscillator, a wavefolder, a mixer and a lowpass gate.

The complex oscillator

An oscillator makes a repeating wave. The pitch of the note is how fast it repeats. FEZ's complex oscillator makes two waves at once, on the same pitch, and blends them:

  • a pure sine wave, which has no harmonics (no overtones above the note), and
  • a shaped wave, which is rich in harmonics. CXWAVE chooses it: the bottom third of the register is a triangle, the middle third a square, and the top third a saw.

CXBLEND mixes them. At 0 you hear only the sine; at full only the shaped wave. The blend keeps the loudness steady as you turn it, so nothing jumps.

The pitch is PITCH, in the units explained in Pitch: 256 to a semitone, with C4 at 15360.

Frequency modulation

A second oscillator, the mod oscillator, can push the pitch of the first up and down very fast. This is frequency modulation (FM). At low speed it adds a wobble or vibrato. At audio speed it makes the clanging, bell-like tones FM is known for. Three registers set it: MDPITCH is the speed, written as a pitch like PITCH (so C3 MDPITCH ! works; the lowest is about 8 Hz), MDWAVE is its wave shape (the quarters of the register give sine, triangle, square and saw), and FMAMT is the depth. The depth is squared, so the bottom of the register is subtle and the top is up to 2000 Hz of swing. The same oscillator is the sound of the mod voice, so retuning one retunes the other.

The wavefolder

A wavefolder takes a wave and, when it gets louder than a limit, bends it back on itself instead of cutting it off. That adds harmonics, and the louder the input the more the wave folds. FOLD sets how hard the oscillator is driven into the folder. Low values leave the sound close to the oscillator; high values make it bright and busy.

The mixer

Three things go into the mixer: the folded complex oscillator (MIXCX, full by default), the mod oscillator itself (MIXMD) and white noise (MIXNZ). White noise is a hiss with equal energy at every frequency. NZTONE is a lowpass on the noise: at the top it is open, and turning it down gives a softer rumble. The mixer has two more levels for the buffer device's output: MIXBP sends it into the lowpass gate, and MIXBF sends it to the effects, never gated. See Devices.

The lowpass gate

Next comes the part that gives the voice its character. A lowpass gate is a filter and a volume control in one, and the same signal drives both. When it is open, the sound passes at full level and bright. As it closes, the sound grows quieter and duller at once, as a plucked string or a struck bell does. It is modelled on the vactrol, a small lamp and light-sensitive resistor used in Buchla synthesisers. The lamp lights quickly and fades slowly, and the fade slows down the closer to dark it gets. That long tail is the sound.

You control it with five registers:

  • GATE: write any non-zero number and the lamp lights. 1 GATE ! plays a note.
  • GATELEVEL: how far the gate stays open all the time. The gate's real opening is GATELEVEL plus the lamp (the envelope), limited to fully open. At 0, the default, the gate is shut between notes and each GATE plays a note. At full the gate is always open and the voice drones, with no note needed. In between, the voice sounds softly all the time and each GATE lifts it. It is an ordinary register, so a matrix route (an LFO, say) can sway it, and a block can set it from code: 20000 GATELEVEL !. It is the way to hold a note open, on the handheld too.
  • ATK: how fast the gate opens, from 1 ms to 10 s.
  • REL: how long the tail lasts, from 10 ms to 4 s.
  • CUTOFF: how bright the sound is when the gate is fully open, from 40 Hz to 14 kHz. As the gate closes, the cutoff falls from here down to 40 Hz.
C3 PITCH !
2000 ATK !          \ a quick attack
28000 REL !         \ a long tail: about 1.7 seconds
26000 CUTOFF !      \ bright when open
1 GATE !            \ play the note

The envelope also exists as a number the matrix can use: ENV rises when the gate fires and falls as the sound fades. Route it to FMAMT and each note starts bright and mellows, which is how Glass Bells works. See the matrix.

A key held on the keyboard holds the gate open, and letting go lets the tail run. Blocks, pulsers and the sequencer fire the gate once and let it fall.

The mod voice

The mod voice plays the mod oscillator, the same one that makes the FM, through its own filter and its own volume, and is never gated. MDPITCH tunes it exactly as PITCH tunes the main voice: 256 to a semitone, C4 is 15360, and ST, HZ and note names all work. Its wave is MDWAVE. The oscillator and the noise are blended by MDNZ (0 is all oscillator, full is all noise). The blend goes through a ladder filter: a lowpass of the kind Moog made, whose steep slope gives a thick, warm roll-off. MDCUT sets where it starts to cut (40 Hz to 14 kHz, scaled like CUTOFF), and MDRES adds resonance, a boost at the cutoff that turns a noise sweep from a hush into a whistle. MDLVL is its volume: 0 is silent, which is why the mod voice does nothing until you raise it.

Low-passed white noise is quiet, so FEZ lifts the noise as the cutoff falls, up to six times, so a slow sweep keeps a steady loudness.

A2 MDPITCH !        \ the mod voice drones on A, under the main voice
12000 MDCUT !
20000 MDLVL !       \ bring the mod voice up

To make the mod oscillator follow the main voice, turn on MDTRACK. MDPITCH then means an interval above PITCH instead of a note of its own: C4 is the same note, G4 a fifth above, C5 an octave above, C3 an octave below, and CTRL shows it in semitones (+7st). It follows whatever the voice actually plays, glide, modulation and quantiser included, so it keeps step with the keys, the sequencer and your blocks. For FM this keeps the ratio between the two oscillators fixed, so the timbre stays the same from the bottom of the keyboard to the top; for the mod voice it is a second voice playing in parallel.

32767 MDTRACK !     \ follow the main voice
C5 MDPITCH !        \ an octave above it
5000 FMAMT !        \ FM at a 2:1 ratio: the same tone on every key

Older versions of FEZ set the mod oscillator's speed with a register called FMRATE. Patches saved by them load with MDPITCH at the same frequency, so they sound as they did, except that FM slower than about 8 Hz becomes 8 Hz.

The master level

LEVEL is the master volume, the first row of the CTRL tab. It comes last in the chain, after the effects and the compressor, so it scales the finished sound. If the output reaches full scale, the CLIP light in the status bar shows for a second.

05Control

A synthesiser that only does what you tell it, when you tell it, is an instrument. One that also acts on its own is closer to a piece of music. This chapter covers the parts that make things happen in time: the pulsers (clocks), the sequencer (a row of notes), the slew generators (smoothing) and the modulation matrix (patch cables that need no cables).

Pulsers

A pulser is a clock that ticks at a steady rate. There are four, numbered 0 to 3. Each has an on/off switch and a rate in pulses per minute, and both are set on the PULSERS tab. At 60 a pulser fires once a second; at 120, twice. Ctrl+P switches all four off and on again without losing their settings.

A pulser does nothing by itself. It fires, and whatever is wired to it responds. Three kinds of thing can be wired:

  • Blocks. Each block has a register, BP0 to BP15, holding a mask: a number whose binary digits say which pulsers run the block. Bit 0 is pulser 0, bit 1 is pulser 1, and so on, so 1 means pulser 0, 2 means pulser 1, and 3 means both. 1 BP0 ! makes pulser 0 run block 0 every time it fires. A block runs once per tick however many pulsers are wired to it and fire together.
  • The sequencer, through SQPUL: each fire moves it one step on (see below).
  • Devices such as the grains (GRPUL), the cellular automaton and the Turing machine (TMPUL), described in Devices.

You can also fire a pulser from code with TRIG: 2 TRIG fires pulser 2 at the next tick. On the desktop, F on the PULSERS tab does the same by hand; on the handheld, the STICKS screen's four buttons do. A key on the KEYS page can fire pulsers too, through KBPUL.

To run a block directly, without a pulser, write its number to RUN: 4 RUN ! runs block 4 at the next tick.

The sequencer

The step sequencer holds eight pitches, SQ0 to SQ7, and plays them in a loop. Each time it is clocked it moves to the next step and does one or two things, which you choose in SQDRV: add 1 to write the step's pitch to PITCH, and add 2 to fire the gate. So 3 does both, which is the usual choice.

  • SQLEN (1 to 8) is how many steps are in the loop.
  • SQEN is a mask of enabled steps, bit n for step n. A disabled step is skipped, which makes rests and shorter patterns easy. If every step is disabled, the sequencer stays where it is.
  • SQSTEP is the current step, 0 to 7.
  • SQCLK: write any non-zero number to clock the sequencer once. SQPUL is the mask of pulsers that clock it.
C4 SQ0 !  E4 SQ1 !  G4 SQ2 !  C5 SQ3 !     \ four notes of a chord
4 SQLEN !                                   \ a loop of four
3 SQDRV !                                   \ set the pitch and play it
1 SQPUL !                                   \ pulser 0 clocks it

With pulser 0 turned on and set to 120, that plays two notes a second, round and round. Pitches are in the units of Pitch, so you can add a semitone offset to a step with ST. Since steps are just registers, a block can rewrite them while the sequence plays.

Slew

Four registers, CV0 to CV3, exist for blocks to write numbers into. They hold -32768 to 32767, can be used as matrix sources, and affect nothing until a route sends them somewhere. A jump in a value is audible as a click or a lurch, so each has a slew: a smoother that makes the change glide. SLT0 to SLT3 set the glide time (1 ms to 5 s; 0 turns the slew off), and the smoothed value appears in SLO0 to SLO3, another matrix source.

The glide is exponential: each step it covers a fixed share of the remaining distance, so it starts fast and finishes slowly, as a real analogue circuit does. This is the way to get a filter to swoop towards a new value instead of jumping.

26000 SLT0 !          \ a glide time of nearly a second
16000 RND CV0 !       \ a random target; SLO0 follows

The modulation matrix

To modulate is to move a setting automatically. The matrix is the switchboard that does it. A route joins a source, something that changes over time, to a destination, a register, with a weight that says how much. Each tick, FEZ computes for every register an effective value:

effective value = the register's own value + (weight ÷ 32768) × the source, then limited to 0 to 32767.

The sound reads the effective value. The register itself is not changed: the CTRL tab shows it, CUTOFF @ reads it, and the sound moves around it. A weight of 32767 passes the whole source, 16384 passes half, and a negative weight turns the source upside down. You can have 16 routes. They are set in the MATRIX tab, or from code with ROUTE:

LFO0 CUTOFF 4000 ROUTE      \ the LFO sways the cutoff
ENV FMAMT 8000 ROUTE        \ each note starts bright
ENV CUTOFF 6000 NEG ROUTE   \ a negative weight

The word takes the source, the destination and the weight, in that order. Routing the same pair again just changes the weight. Any register that shapes the sound can be a destination, except GATE. A full matrix, or an unknown source or destination, is a fault.

The sources

Most sources are named by the register that holds them. Three have a different name in code, shown in the last column.

SourceWhat it isRangeName in ROUTE
LFO0a slow sine wave, 0.05 Hz to 20 Hz (LFORATE)-32767 to 32767LFO0
ENVthe envelope: rises when the gate fires, falls over REL0 to 32767ENV
CV0 to CV3numbers written by blocks-32768 to 32767CV0 to CV3
MP0 to MP15sixteen read-only registers for knobs and controllers: the program cannot write them, only the outside world can (on the Brick, the two sticks are MP0 to MP3)0 to 32767MP0 to MP15
SLO0 to SLO3CV0 to CV3, smoothed-32768 to 32767SLO0 to SLO3
CADENShow full the cellular automaton row is0 to 32767CADENS
LZX, LZY, LZZthe three axes of the Lorenz attractorsignedLZX, LZY, LZZ
SQthe current sequencer step's pitch, relative to C4 (one semitone is 2048)signedSQOUT
TMthe Turing machine's output0 to 32767TMOUT
KBthe key held on the keyboard, relative to C4; 0 when nonesignedKBNOTE

The devices (CADENS, Lorenz, TM) are explained in Devices. The quantiser, which can snap the effective pitch to a scale, acts after the matrix: it sees the pitch with modulation added, never the PITCH register itself.

A good first route is the one that gives a sound life: send the slow LFO to a cutoff with a small weight. Nothing is added to the code and nothing needs to fire. The sound moves on its own.

06Devices

A device is a small machine inside FEZ that produces change by itself. It has no sound of its own. It makes numbers: a row of bits that evolves, a curve that never repeats, a melody that drifts. You use those numbers by routing them through the matrix, reading them in a block, or letting a device fire a pulser when something happens. Each device has a page on the DEVICES tab (move between pages with [ and ]).

Here is the idea behind all of them. A sound that is perfectly steady is dull, and one that is perfectly random is noise. Music lives in between: patterns that nearly repeat. The devices are different ways of producing that.

Cellular automaton

Picture a row of 16 cells, each on or off, joined in a ring. At each generation every cell looks at itself and its two neighbours, which gives three bits, or a number from 0 to 7. A rule says what the cell becomes for each of the eight patterns. The rule is itself a number from 0 to 255, one bit for each pattern, and it is held in CARULE. Rule 30 produces a tangled, unpredictable-looking pattern from almost nothing, and rule 90 draws triangles. The row is CAROW, one bit per cell.

  • CASTEP: write a number from 1 to 16 to run that many generations. 1 CASTEP ! runs one. On the DEVICES page, Space does it.
  • CATAP picks one cell to watch (0 to 15) and CABIT reads its state.
  • CATRIG picks a pulser (0 to 3) to fire when the watched cell is born, which means it was off and is now on. 4 means none.
  • CACOUNT is the number of live cells, and CADENS is the same as a proportion, for the matrix. Both are read only.

A worked example: pulser 0 runs one generation every beat, and each birth at the watched cell fires pulser 1, which plays a note picked from the low four bits of the row. The notes come from a pentatonic colour, so they sound right together.

\ block 0, run by pulser 0: advance the automaton
1 CASTEP !
\ block 1, run by pulser 1: play a note from the row
CAROW @ 15 AND 13 COLOUR C3 + PITCH !
1 GATE !
\ any block, run once: wire it up
1 BP0 !         \ pulser 0 runs block 0
2 BP1 !         \ pulser 1 runs block 1
1 CATRIG !      \ a birth fires pulser 1

Turn pulser 0 on at 120 pulses a minute. COLOUR turns a number into a note of a five-note scale: the first number steps up the scale, and the second chooses the flavour, 0 to 15. The word reference explains it in full.

Lorenz attractor

The Lorenz attractor is three numbers that chase each other according to three equations from a weather model of 1963. The path they trace never repeats, but it stays within bounds and loops lazily round two lobes, like a butterfly's wings. That makes it a good slow, smooth, unpredictable modulator.

  • LZX, LZY and LZZ are the three values, read only. All three are matrix sources.
  • LZRATE sets the speed.
  • LZRHO sets a parameter of the equations. About 28 gives the classic chaotic path; lower values make the path settle towards a fixed point instead of wandering.
  • LZTRIG picks a pulser to fire each time X crosses zero, which is each time the path swaps lobes. 4 means none.
  • LZSEED: write any number to restart the path from a new place.
LZX CUTOFF 6000 ROUTE        \ the filter wanders
LZZ FOLD 4000 ROUTE

Quantiser

To quantise is to round to the nearest allowed value. The quantiser rounds the pitch to the nearest note of a scale. That is how a wandering signal, such as an LFO or the Lorenz attractor, can control a pitch and still sound like music.

  • QON: any non-zero number turns it on.
  • QSCALE chooses the scale: 0 chromatic, 1 major, 2 natural minor, 3 dorian, 4 major pentatonic, 5 minor pentatonic, 6 blues, 7 whole tone.
  • QROOT is the note the scale is built on, written like a pitch: C3 QROOT !.

It works on the pitch the voice hears, after the matrix adds its modulation. It does not touch the PITCH register. So the register can hold any number and the sound still lands on the scale. A note exactly between two scale notes goes to the lower.

1 QON !
4 QSCALE !                   \ major pentatonic
C3 QROOT !
LFO0 PITCH 3000 ROUTE        \ an octave each way, in key

Turing machine

This is a loop of bits that rewrites itself slowly. It holds up to 16 bits in a ring. At each step the oldest bit is taken, flipped with some chance, and put back in as the newest. If the chance is 0, nothing is ever flipped and the pattern repeats exactly. If it is high, the pattern is random. In between, a melody emerges that nearly repeats and changes a little each time round.

  • TMLEN: how many bits are in the loop, 2 to 16. The loop length is the length of the repeating phrase.
  • TMCHANCE: the chance that a bit flips. 0 never; 16384 is a coin toss (fully random); the default 4096 is about one in eight.
  • TMSTEP: write any non-zero number to take a step. TMPUL is a mask of the pulsers that step it.
  • TMBITS: the bits themselves. Writing sets them.
  • TMOUT: the newest eight bits (or all, if the loop is shorter) read as a number, 0 to 32767. It is a matrix source.
1 TMPUL !                    \ pulser 0 steps the machine
TMOUT PITCH 6000 ROUTE       \ the bits pick the pitch
1 QON !  4 QSCALE !          \ keep it in key

Lock the pattern by setting 0 TMCHANCE !, and loosen it a little at a time.

Keyboard

The keyboard device turns key presses into notes. On the desktop, the KEYS tab plays the computer keyboard like a piano: the bottom row (Z S X D C V G B H N J M) is one octave, and the row above (Q 2 W 3 E R 5 T 6 Y 7 U) is the next. The layout follows the position of the keys, so it works on any national layout. Only that tab plays, and Space lets go of everything. The handheld has no KEYS tab; its STICKS screen plays the keyboard device from the left stick instead (see the handheld chapter).

A key press does four things: it writes the note into PITCH and KBNOTE, fires the gate, fires the pulsers in the mask KBPUL, and holds the gate open until the key is let go, then the release runs. If you press a second key while the first is held, the new one wins, and letting go of it returns to the first without a new attack. KBOCT (0 to 8) is the octave of the bottom key, and KBGATE is 1 while any key is down. KBNOTE and KBGATE are read only; KBNOTE is also a matrix source, which can be used to make a filter follow the notes you play.

KBNOTE CUTOFF 2000 ROUTE     \ higher notes sound brighter

07Space and time

This chapter is about the end of the signal path: the effects that make a sound last, and the buffer that records it. FEZ is built for slow music in the manner of Fripp and Eno, where a few notes are played into a tape loop and come round again, quieter and darker, for minutes. The effects and the buffer are the instruments for that.

The order matters. The voice, the mod voice and whatever the buffer plays back all go into the tape delay. Its output goes into the spring reverb, then a compressor, then the master LEVEL. The figure in the overview shows it.

The tape delay

A delay repeats a sound after a time. A tape delay does it with a loop of tape: each time round, the sound is copied back, a little duller and a little less steady. FEZ's delay keeps these faults on purpose.

  • DLYTIME: the length of the loop, from 0 to 12 seconds. The scale is a straight line, 0.37 ms for each step of the register, so 19930 is 7.3 seconds. The default, 814, is 0.3 seconds.
  • DLYFB: feedback, how much of the loop is fed back into itself. 0 gives one echo, and values near the top give echoes that go on for minutes. There is no cap: at the maximum a sound should neither die nor grow. Inside the loop, loud sounds are gently squashed so that it cannot run away.
  • DLYMIX: the balance of dry and wet. At 0, where a blank patch starts, you hear only the dry sound. As you raise it the dry fades as the echoes rise, and at full you hear only the loop.
  • DLYIN: how much of the new sound is written onto the loop. Full is the default. Lower values let new notes lie gently over the old ones instead of drowning them, and 0 closes the loop so that nothing new goes in. The scale is squared, so there is plenty of room at the quiet end.
  • DLYLP: a lowpass filter in the loop, 300 Hz to 12 kHz. Each trip round takes off more treble, so old sound fades to a murmur.
  • DLYWOB: wow and flutter, the slow and fast wavering of a tape's speed. It bends the pitch of the echoes a little.
  • DLYNZ: tape hiss, written into the loop. It adds a little more each trip.
  • DLYFRZ: freeze. At or above 16384 the loop stops listening and holds an exact copy of itself: no new sound, no hiss, no filtering. A frozen loop does not fade. You can play over it, and let go to return to normal.
19930 DLYTIME !     \ 7.3 seconds round
29000 DLYFB !       \ nearly 89 percent feedback
18000 DLYLP !       \ each trip round is darker
3000 DLYWOB !       \ a trace of wow
22000 DLYIN !       \ new notes lie over the old

The patch Deep Loop is built this way. To freeze it, go to the DELAY page of the DEVICES tab and press Space, or write 32767 DLYFRZ !.

The spring reverb

A reverb adds the sense of a room. A spring reverb was originally a coiled spring in a guitar amplifier, and has a bright, springy, slightly metallic ring. FEZ's is made of two short loops, one for each ear, tuned apart so that the left and right sounds differ.

  • SPRMIX: how much of the reverb you hear. A blank patch starts at 0, dry.
  • SPRDEC: how long it takes to die away.
  • SPRWID: the stereo width. At 0 both ears hear the same, and at full the two sides are as different as they can be, which makes the room seem wide.
  • SPRTONE: how metallic it is. At 0 each loop repeats one clean copy of the sound every few hundredths of a second, which rings like a tin can: the classic, boingy spring. Raising it smears each repeat into a spread of smaller ones, softens the pitches the spring rings at, and lets the loops drift a little so those pitches never settle. At full it is a soft wash. A blank patch starts halfway; patches saved before SPRTONE existed load at 0, the spring they were made with.

The compressor

Stacked loops can build up into something loud. A compressor turns down the loud parts, so the quiet parts can stay clear. FEZ's has no controls: it works above -10 dB, reduces the excess to an eighth, and reacts in 3 milliseconds. Its job is to keep a thick patch from overloading the output, not to change the sound. If the CLIP light still comes on, lower LEVEL.

The buffer

The delay is a loop of fixed length. The buffer is a store of recent sound that you can reach into at any point. It is a ring of up to 30 seconds (BUFMS sets the length, 50 ms to 30000 ms; the default is 2 seconds). A write head records into the ring, and when it reaches the end it wraps round and overwrites the oldest sound. Eight read voices play from the ring.

Recording

  • BWMODE: 0 means the head is frozen (it holds what it has), 1 means it records all the time, and 2 means a one-shot. The default is 1.
  • BWSRC: what the head hears. 0 is the mixer (the voice, the mod oscillator and noise, before the gate), 1 is the voice after the gate, 2 is the mod voice, and 3 is both of those together.
  • BIN: the record level.
  • BWFB: feedback from the read voices back into the head, so that sounds keep going round. It is soft clipped, so 100 percent is safe.
  • A one-shot clears the buffer and records once, for the length BWLEN (a proportion of the buffer, full by default). Write any non-zero number to BWTRIG to start one.

On the BUFFER tab, R records a one-shot, F freezes the head, S stops the voices, C clears the buffer and Space triggers the voices. The buffer audio is not saved with a patch, and loading a patch empties it.

Read voices

Each of the eight voices has five registers, numbered 0 to 7: GPOS (position), GRATE (rate), GLEN (length), GLVL (level) and GFLG (flags). A voice with no level is silent. A voice works in one of two ways, decided by its length.

A continuous voice (GLEN of 0) plays all the time. Its position is a proportion of the buffer, 0 to 32767. If the flag REL is set, it is a tap that sits that far behind the write head, which makes it a delay: 9830 GPOS0 ! with REL reads sound from nine seconds ago in a 30-second buffer. Without it, the voice is a free-running loop that starts at that position and plays round the ring at the speed GRATE sets.

A grain (GLEN above 0) plays a short snippet, that many milliseconds long, then stops. GTRIG is a mask of the voices to start, and the pulsers named in GRPUL start the next grain each time they fire, going round the voices in turn. A grain has a window, a fade in and out so there is no click: GWIN goes from a rectangle (with very short edges) to a smooth Hann curve. Many grains close together make a cloud of sound, which is how the Grain Cloud patch works.

GRATE is written as a pitch: C4 (15360) plays at the original speed, and each octave (3072) up doubles the speed and raises the pitch of the sound, within four octaves either way. The flags are added together: 1 REL (position is behind the head), 2 REV (play backwards), 4 TRK (follow the pitch of the voice, so the buffer can be played like an instrument) and 8 LOOP (a grain repeats until stopped, and GSTOP stops it).

Only voice 0 can be modulated by the matrix (GPOS0, GRATE0 and GLVL0); the other seven use their plain register values.

Getting the sound back

The voices' sum is the buffer's output. MIXBF sends it to the effects, never gated. MIXBP sends it into the lowpass gate instead, so it is shaped by the same envelope as the voice.

A tape-loop patch, step by step

Here is the heart of Deep Loop. The voice plays rarely, softly and slowly. The buffer records the voice, and four read voices play it back from 9, 14, 21 and 27 seconds ago, which means that old phrases are fed back into the delay at distances that never line up.

\ the buffer records the voice, 30 seconds of it
30000 BUFMS !
1 BWSRC !

\ four taps behind the write head, quieter the further back
9830 GPOS0 !   1 GFLG0 !   9000 GLVL0 !     \ 9 seconds
15291 GPOS1 !  1 GFLG1 !   8000 GLVL1 !     \ 14 seconds
22937 GPOS2 !  1 GFLG2 !   7000 GLVL2 !     \ 21 seconds
29490 GPOS3 !  1 GFLG3 !   6000 GLVL3 !     \ 27 seconds
16000 MIXBF !                               \ send them on

\ the tape loop itself
19930 DLYTIME !  29000 DLYFB !  18000 DLYLP !  22000 DLYIN !

The voice, set to a long attack and release with a soft sine, is played by two pulsers a few seconds apart, each running a block that acts one time in three or four. Start from the example, and change one number at a time: DLYIN for how thickly the loop layers, DLYFB for how long it lasts, DLYLP for how dark it gets.

08Playing it

This chapter is about the desktop app: what is on the screen, how to move around it, and which key does what. (The handheld has its own chapter.) FEZ has no mouse support. Everything is done from the keyboard, so that it works as well on a laptop in a dark room as on a small screen on a Raspberry Pi.

The window

The window is cut into tiles, and each tile shows one tab. The tile with the amber frame has the focus, which means it receives your keys. A layout is one way of cutting the window up; there are three, numbered 1, 2 and 3 like workspaces in a tiling window manager, and Ctrl+Tab moves to the next. Each tile starts on a tab that suits the layout, and you can change any tile's tab:

  • Layout 1: the editor on the left, the scope and the CTRL list on the right. For writing.
  • Layout 2: two tiles of equal width, the editor on the left and the CTRL list on the right. For writing and turning knobs side by side.
  • Layout 3: the scope along the top, the CTRL list and the devices below. For listening to a patch that plays itself.

Move the focus between tiles with Ctrl+Arrows. Change the tab in the focused tile with Ctrl+[ and Ctrl+]. Inside a tab, plain [ and ] move to the previous or next page: the next block in the editor, the next list in PATCHES, the next device in DEVICES. (This is why the editor cannot type square brackets: they are never needed, and the keys are worth more as page turners.) Alt works like Ctrl everywhere, for keyboards where Ctrl is awkward. Ctrl+= and Ctrl+- make the text bigger and smaller, Ctrl+F goes full screen, and Ctrl+Q quits. F1 shows every key on one page.

The status bar at the bottom shows the layout, the patch name, whether the pulsers are on, a short message about what you just did, and, at the right, the CPU load and the CLIP light. The CPU bar is the time the audio takes as a share of the time it has; green is under 70 percent, amber to 90 and red above. The thin marker on it is the worst moment in the last three seconds. Every example patch uses about 1 percent on an ordinary laptop. CLIP comes on for a second when the output reaches full scale.

The tabs

  • EDITOR: sixteen blocks of code. See below.
  • PATCHES: load, save and delete. See Patches.
  • CTRL: every register in one list, under group headings, starting with the master volume. Up and Down pick a row; Left and Right change it (Shift for big steps); type digits and press Enter to set an exact value. Tab switches between real units (Hz, seconds, percent) and raw register numbers.
  • DEVICES: pages for the delay, the cellular automaton, Lorenz, the quantiser and the Turing machine. Space does the page's main action (a step, a reseed, a freeze).
  • BUFFER: the tape, and its voices.
  • PULSERS: the four clocks. Space toggles one, F fires it, and you can type a new rate.
  • SEQ: the eight steps. Type a note name to set a step, and press Enter to clock the sequencer once.
  • MATRIX: the routes. Enter picks or adjusts a cell, and Backspace deletes a route.
  • KEYS: the computer keyboard as a piano (see below).
  • STICKS: only while a gamepad is plugged in. Its left stick plays the notes of a scale, and A, B, X and Y fire pulsers 0 to 3, exactly as on the handheld (see the STICKS screen).
  • SCOPE: a picture of the output wave, steadied by starting each sweep on a rising edge.

The editor

The editor holds sixteen blocks, one at a time. [ and ] move between them. Each block keeps its own text, and the text you are typing never touches the sound until you apply it. This is deliberate, so that a half-typed program cannot do anything.

  • Ctrl+Enter applies the block: it compiles the text and swaps it in. A mistake is shown in red with the line, and the word that failed is marked with a red block in the text. The old version keeps running. A fault that halted the block is cleared by applying it again.
  • Ctrl+R applies the block and runs it once, now. If it does not compile, nothing runs and the mistake is marked.
  • Ctrl+1 to Ctrl+4 switch on or off whether pulsers 0 to 3 run this block.
  • Tab completes the word you are typing, and cycles through the matches if there are several.
  • Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Y undo and redo. Ctrl+C, Ctrl+X and Ctrl+V copy, cut and paste.
  • There are no Home, End or Page keys: the arrows are enough for blocks of 128 slots at the most.

Making a sound

  • Ctrl+G fires the gate, once: one note.
  • Ctrl+P switches the four pulsers off and on together, remembering which were on.
  • Shift+Esc mutes and unmutes, with a 20 millisecond fade. The synth keeps running underneath. Plain Esc only cancels something you are typing.
  • Ctrl+T starts and stops a recording of the final output. See below.

The KEYS tab

To play FEZ as an instrument, go to the KEYS tab (Ctrl+] moves through the tabs). The computer keyboard now plays notes, laid out like a piano, by the position of each key so that it works on any national layout:

  2 3   5 6 7          upper octave: black keys
 Q W E R T Y U         upper octave: white keys
  S D   G H J          lower octave: black keys
 Z X C V B N M         lower octave: white keys

The notes are Z (C), S (C sharp), X (D), D (D sharp), C (E), V (F), G (F sharp), B (G), H (G sharp), N (A), J (A sharp) and M (B), and the upper row is the next octave, starting on Q. Space lets go of every key. Only this tab plays; the rest of the time the letters are for typing. If the window loses focus, every held note is released. How a key behaves is explained in the keyboard device.

A gamepad

Plug in a gamepad and the STICKS tab appears. Its two sticks are the modulation pots MP0 to MP3 on every tab (left stick left and right is MP0, up and down MP1; the right stick MP2 and MP3), and on the STICKS tab the left stick plays notes instead while A, B, X and Y fire the pulsers. The buttons go by the labels of an Xbox pad: A, B, X and Y are pulsers 0, 1, 2 and 3. Use the keyboard for the tab's settings. Unplug the pad and the tab leaves the tab bar.

Sound output and MIDI: F2

Press F2 for the setup page. It covers the window, like the help page, and F2 or Esc closes it. Up and Down move through everything on it. Your choices are saved in ~/FEZ/setup.txt as soon as you make them, and come back the next time FEZ starts. They are not part of any patch, because they describe your computer and your controllers, not a sound.

  • AUDIO OUTPUT: the sound devices. Enter on one sends the sound there; default follows whatever the system uses. If the saved device is missing when FEZ starts, for example because it is unplugged, the sound goes to the default instead.
  • MIDI INPUT: the MIDI devices. Enter on one listens to it, and none stops listening. Notes play the keyboard device, just as the KEYS tab does, so KBNOTE, KBGATE and the KBPUL pulsers follow them.
  • CHANNEL: Left and Right choose the MIDI channel FEZ hears, 1 to 16, or every one.
  • LAST MESSAGE: the most recent thing the input sent, such as CC 74 = 90 ch 1. Turn a knob and read its controller number here.
  • POTS: the sixteen modulation pots, MP0 to MP15, which the matrix can route anywhere. For each pot, choose which MIDI controller number (CC) moves it: Left and Right step it (with Shift, by ten), or type the number and press Enter. Below 0 is off. A bar shows where each pot is now.

Space on a pot changes how its controller is read, because knobs and endless encoders send different things:

  • abs: an ordinary knob or fader. It sends its position, 0 at the bottom to 127 at the top.
  • rel64: an endless encoder that sends 64 plus the number of clicks it turned, so 65 is one click up and 63 one click down. Some makers call this "binary offset".
  • rel2c: an endless encoder that sends 1 for one click up and 127 for one click down ("two's complement").

If an encoder makes its pot jump to the top or bottom, it is not in abs mode. If it moves the pot the wrong way, or only one way, try the other relative mode. The LAST MESSAGE line shows what it sends as you turn it. With an encoder, 128 clicks take a pot from bottom to top.

On macOS and Windows every MIDI input the system knows about is listed. On Linux FEZ lists ALSA's raw MIDI ports, which covers USB and hardware devices. A software port, such as a virtual keyboard, only appears there if it is connected to a virtual raw port; the snd-virmidi module provides those. If you plug a device in while the page is open, press R to look again.

Recording a take

Press Ctrl+T. The status bar shows REC, and FEZ writes what you hear, after the mute, to a 24-bit stereo WAV file in ~/FEZ/recordings/, named by date, time and patch, such as 2026-11-25_114302_Deep Loop.wav (the seconds keep two quick takes apart). Press Ctrl+T again to stop. The audio is passed to the disk by a separate thread, so recording cannot cause a glitch in the sound.

All the keys

KeyWhat it does
Ctrl+Arrowsmove to the tile that way
Ctrl+[ and Ctrl+]previous and next tab
[ and ]previous and next page inside a tab
Ctrl+Tabnext layout
Up, Down, Left, Rightpick a row, change a value (Shift: big steps)
0 to 9, Entertype an exact number, store it
Esccancel what you are typing
Ctrl+= and Ctrl+-bigger and smaller text
Ctrl+Ffull screen on and off
Ctrl+Qquit
Ctrl+Gfire the gate: play one note
Ctrl+Ppulsers on and off
Shift+Escmute and unmute
Ctrl+Ssave the patch (asks for a name)
Ctrl+Ddelete the picked patch (asks first)
Ctrl+Nstart a blank patch (asks first)
Ctrl+Tstart or stop recording
Ctrl+Enter, Ctrl+Rin the editor: apply the block; apply it and run it once
F1the help page

09The handheld

FEZ runs on the TrimUI Brick, a pocket game console with a 1024 by 768 screen, a d-pad, four face buttons, four shoulder buttons and no keyboard. The same program runs on it: the buttons are translated into the keys the desktop uses, so everything described in the other chapters is there. This chapter explains how the buttons map to it, and how to put FEZ on the device.

The screen is drawn at 256 by 192 and scaled up by four, in large pixels, with the same colours as the desktop. It shows one screen at a time, instead of a window of tiles. The face buttons are laid out as on a Nintendo pad: A is the right one, B the bottom, X the top and Y the left.

Putting FEZ on the Brick

FEZ needs a launcher on the Brick that can start programs from the card; it was developed on NextUI, a replacement firmware, and the same folder layout works on MinUI. A program is a folder called a pak, with a script named launch.sh in it.

  1. Build the pak. On the computer, brick/build.sh cross-compiles FEZ for the Brick's ARM processor inside a container (it needs Docker, or Colima on a Mac) and leaves dist/FEZ.pak.
  2. Copy the folder FEZ.pak onto the card, into Tools/tg5040/.
  3. Put the card in the Brick. FEZ appears in the Tools menu. Start it.

FEZ keeps its files on the card in a folder called FEZ: patches in FEZ/patches/ and recordings in FEZ/recordings/. They are plain files, so you can copy them to a computer, or from one. If FEZ does not start, look at fez.log in the pak folder: it holds whatever the program printed.

The buttons that work everywhere

  • L1 and R1: the previous and next screen.
  • L2 and R2 (the lower shoulder buttons): the previous and next page on a screen, as [ and ] do on the desktop.
  • D-pad: move, and change values. Hold Y as well to take big steps, as Shift does on the desktop.
  • Start: fire the gate, to play one note.
  • Select: mute and unmute.
  • Volume + and -: the master volume.
  • Menu: open the menu (see below).
  • A, B and X: the three buttons whose job depends on the screen. A line at the bottom of the screen always says what they do.

The analogue sticks

The two sticks are knobs. Each direction of each stick is one of the first four modulation pots (see the matrix), on every screen but one: on the STICKS screen the left stick plays notes instead (see below).

  • Left stick: left and right is MP0, up and down is MP1.
  • Right stick: left and right is MP2, up and down is MP3.

At rest a stick holds its pot at the middle of the range, 16384. Push right or up and the pot rises towards 32767; push left or down and it falls towards 0. A small dead zone around the centre keeps a stick that does not quite return to zero from nudging the sound. The pots do nothing until you route them. To make the left stick open the filter, send MP0 to CUTOFF in the matrix:

MP0 CUTOFF 16384 ROUTE      \ left-right sweeps the cutoff

Loading a patch leaves the pots where they are, because they belong to your hands and not to the patch. The CTRL screen shows all sixteen under the POTS heading. MP4 to MP15 are not connected to anything yet.

Playing tunes: the STICKS screen

The STICKS screen turns the handheld into an instrument: the left stick plays notes, and A, B, X and Y fire pulsers 0 to 3, so the right hand can set off blocks, the sequencer or grains while the left plays. A pad for each button lights up when its pulser fires. The right stick stays a pair of pots.

The left stick's Its direction picks a note: straight up is the root, and each eighth of a turn clockwise is the next note of the scale, so the eight directions are the first eight notes. In a seven-note scale, up-left is the octave; in a five-note colour, the octave is down-left. The screen draws the eight notes in a ring (for colours, their degree numbers, 0 to 7), with the root in green and the one you are holding lit. While this screen is showing, the left stick does not modulate: MP0 and MP1 keep the values they had when you arrived, so anything routed from them holds steady while you play, and on another screen the stick sets them again the next time it moves.

Four settings choose the notes and how they sound. Up and Down pick one, and Left and Right change it:

  • TYPE (STKTYPE): scales (0), the quantiser's eight, as the word SCALE gives them; or colours (1), the sixteen five-note scales in just intonation that the word COLOUR gives.
  • SCALE (STKSCALE): which scale (0 to 7, major by default) or which colour (0 to 15).
  • ROOT (STKROOT): the note straight up plays, C4 by default, as on the quantiser page. Left and right step a semitone; with Y held, a fifth.
  • MODE (STKMODE): how a note sounds, play or swell. The Menu's first tab can switch it too.

In play mode (0) the stick works like a key. Pushing it out plays the note with a fresh attack, moving round to another direction plays the next note, and letting the stick spring back lets go, so the release runs. Because it goes through the keyboard device, KBNOTE, KBGATE and the pulsers in KBPUL follow the stick as they follow keys. A colour's just notes fall between the keys: KBNOTE holds the nearest key, and PITCH the exact note.

In swell mode (1) the direction only moves PITCH, with no attack, and how far you push sets GATELEVEL, which holds the gate open by hand. Push gently for a quiet note, push to the edge for full volume, and let the stick return to fade it out. Turning the stick round while it is pushed out glides through the scale without a break. Swell mode owns GATELEVEL: leaving the screen or switching mode sets it back to 0.

Near the border between two directions the stick keeps the note it has until you are clearly past the border, so a note does not flicker between two.

The screens, and what A, B and X do on each

ScreenABX
Editoropen the word palettedelete the last wordapply the block
Patchesload the picked patchdelete it (asks first)save (asks for a name)
Controlstep the value up (fires a write-only register)step it downunits or raw numbers
Matrixpick or adjust a cellcanceldelete the route
Sticksfire pulser 0fire pulser 1fire pulser 2 (Y fires pulser 3)
Devices, Buffer, Pulsers, SequencerEnter: pick or adjustEsc: cancelSpace: the screen's main action (step, freeze, toggle)
Scopea picture of the sound; no actions

The bottom line of each screen says what X does there, and on the Devices screen it changes with the page (X steps the automaton, freezes the delay, and so on).

Writing code without a keyboard

With no keyboard, code is built by picking words from a palette. In the editor, press A. A grid of words opens. L2 and R2 switch the page of the palette:

  • STACK, MATHS, LOGIC, MEMORY and FLOW: the words of the language, grouped by what they do.
  • NOTES: C1 to B5.
  • NUMS: the digits 0 to 9 and a few common numbers. Digits stick together as you pick them (1, then 2, makes 12), and ENT ends the number. There is no minus sign: write 5 NEG.
  • REGS: every register, under its group heading.
  • PULSERS: the names P0 to P3.

Move round the grid with the d-pad. A puts the word at the cursor in your program, B closes the palette, X applies the block and Y deletes the last word. Spaces and line breaks are put in for you.

The menu

Press Menu for a box with two tabs. The first tab carries the name of the screen you are on (EDITOR, say) and lists the extra things that screen can do. MENU holds the things that belong to the whole machine. Left and Right (or L1 and R1) switch tabs, Up and Down pick, A chooses, and B closes the box (or, inside Go to screen, goes back one step). A screen with no extra actions, such as Scope, opens on the MENU tab.

  • Selecting and copying: in the editor, hold Y and use the D-pad to select text, as Shift does on the desktop. Then open the menu and choose Copy or Cut; move the cursor, even to another block, and choose Paste. B deletes the selection if there is one, and otherwise the last word.
  • screen's own tab: extra things the current screen can do that do not fit on A, B and X. On the editor these are run the block once, undo, redo, copy, cut, paste, clear the block, and four tick boxes that say which pulsers run this block. Other screens have theirs: on Buffer, trigger, stop, record, freeze and clear; on Devices, next and previous page and the reseed actions.
  • MENU tab, Go to screen: jump straight to any screen.
  • New blank patch: throw the current patch away and start empty. It takes you to the Patches screen and opens a question box: A yes, B no. Deleting or replacing a saved patch asks the same way.
  • Record to WAV: start or stop a recording.
  • Pulsers: switch them all off or on.
  • Button help: a list of these buttons, on the device.
  • Quit: leave FEZ and return to the launcher.

Saving a patch

On the Patches screen, press X. A name picker opens: Up and Down move through the letters one at a time, Left and Right by five. A adds the letter, B removes the last one, X saves, and Y gives up. The patch goes into FEZ/patches/ on the card. As on the desktop, nothing is saved automatically.

What the Brick does not do

  • There is no KEYS screen. The STICKS screen takes its place: the left stick plays the notes of a scale.
  • The handheld screens are smaller, so a few details, such as the longest register help lines, are shortened.

10Patches

A patch is the whole state of FEZ at one moment: every register, the sixteen blocks and words, the four pulsers, the matrix routes and the devices' settings. Loading a patch replaces all of it, and empties the buffer, the delay, the spring and the compressor, so that nothing from the last patch rings on.

Loading, saving and sharing

On the PATCHES tab there are two lists. MY PATCHES holds the files in ~/FEZ/patches/, and EXAMPLES holds the thirteen that come built in. Left and Right (or [ and ]) switch lists, typing letters narrows the list, Up and Down pick, and Enter loads. Ctrl+S saves the current state under a name, from any tab, and always asks for the name; if the name exists, it asks before overwriting. Ctrl+D or Delete removes a patch, after asking. Ctrl+N throws the current patch away and starts a blank one, from any tab; it asks first, because nothing is saved automatically. On the handheld the same thing is New blank patch on the Menu's MENU tab, and on the PATCHES tab of the Patches screen; answer with A for yes and B for no.

FEZ never saves by itself. A patch you have not saved is gone when you quit. This is a choice: it means the example you load is always the one you hear, and your own patches change only when you say so.

The patch file

A patch is a plain text file, named after the patch with the ending .fez. You can read it, edit it in any text editor, keep it in version control or mail it to a friend. This is the shape, with comments added here for explanation:

FEZ PATCH 1
name Deep Loop
desc Frippertronics at ambient speed...
listen Soft notes that return minutes later
level 16384                 the master level
pulser 0 on 1 rate 10       number, on or off, pulses a minute
reg CUTOFF 12000            a register, by name (only if not default)
reg DLYFB 29000
route ENV CUTOFF 6000       source, destination, weight
ca 30 10836 0 4             automaton: rule, row, tap, trigger
lz 8000 15300 4             Lorenz: rate, rho, trigger
block 0                     its code; lines start "> "
> 3 RND 0 =  1 JZ
> ...
word 2                      the same for a word

Only registers that differ from the defaults are written, so a file stays short, and registers are stored by name, so a patch keeps working if a register ever moves. Blank lines and lines beginning with # are ignored. A line FEZ does not understand is skipped, and the patch loads without it; the status bar says how many were skipped. A file that is not a patch at all is refused.

What is not saved is whatever is only in motion: the audio in the buffer, the position of the sequencer, the phase of the LFO and the envelope. A patch starts from rest, as the built-in ones do.

Making your own

Start from the blank patch, which is what FEZ loads at first, or from one of the examples, and change one thing at a time. A good order is:

  1. Make one note you like with the CTRL tab: pitch, wave, filter, envelope.
  2. Write a block that plays it, and apply and run it with Ctrl+R.
  3. Wire the block to a pulser: Ctrl+1 in the editor, and switch the pulser on and set its rate on the PULSERS tab.
  4. Add one moving thing: a matrix route from the LFO or the envelope.
  5. Add space: the delay and the spring.
  6. Save it with Ctrl+S.

For a patch that plays itself for an hour, build it as Deep Loop does: few notes, long envelopes, and the delay doing most of the work.

11The example patches

FEZ comes with thirteen patches, built in and listed under EXAMPLES on the PATCHES tab. Each one is meant to show something. Load one, listen, then open the editor and read its blocks. This chapter lists them and takes three apart.

The thirteen

In order:

PatchWhat you hearWhat it teaches
Glass Bellsrandom bells over two octaves, long tailsCOLOUR and RND for notes; ENV routed to FM depth
Acid Linea squelchy bass, accents on steps 1, 4 and 7a step pattern kept in scratch registers; accents made by shifting a bit mask, with no branch
Rule 30 Rainirregular drops, brighter when the automaton is crowdedthe cellular automaton firing a pulser
Dub Staboffbeat stabs smeared into echoesthe tape delay; turn DLYFB up
Lorenz Walka melody that never repeats but stays in one scaleLorenz as a note source, and as modulation
Four Pulsersa slowly shifting polyrhythmfour pulsers, each on its own rate
Mod Dronea breathing drone with bell-like notes over itthe mod voice and the ladder filter
Step Melodyan eight-step line that loses and regains notesthe sequencer mask SQEN
Tape Echoplucks followed by two echoes that drift in pitch like tapethe buffer as a delay line (two read voices at 375 and 562 ms); the LFO moves one through the matrix
Grain Cloudslow notes smeared into a shimmering cloudgrains from the buffer
Noise Sweepsa wash of filtered noise rising and fallingthe mod voice's noise through the ladder filter
Ambient Loopssoft notes returning at odd intervalsthe buffer as a tape loop
Deep Loopphrases that return minutes later, dimmerlong delay, low DLYIN and four read voices

Three of them, line by line

Glass Bells

One block, run by pulser 0. Each time it runs it chooses a random note and plays it:

\ bell: random degree 0..9 of colour 10 over C3
10 RND 10 COLOUR C3 + PITCH !
6000 RND 4000 + FMAMT !
1 GATE !
  • 10 RND picks a whole number from 0 to 9. 10 COLOUR turns it into a note of the minor pentatonic scale: 0 to 4 are the first octave, 5 to 9 the next. The result is a distance above the root.
  • C3 + adds the root. PITCH ! stores the pitch.
  • 6000 RND 4000 + is a random number from 4000 to 9999, stored as the FM depth, so each bell has a slightly different brightness.
  • 1 GATE ! plays it.

The patch also has a matrix route that sends the envelope to FMAMT (see the matrix), so the bell starts bright and mellows, and a second block, run by pulser 1, that changes the amount of delay now and then.

Rule 30 Rain

\ block 0 (pulser 0): reseed if dead, then step
CACOUNT @ 1 JNZ  0x0100 CAROW !  1 L
1 CASTEP !
  • CACOUNT @ is the number of living cells. 1 JNZ jumps to label 1 if it is not zero, skipping the reseed. If the automaton has died out, 0x0100 CAROW ! puts a single live cell in the row to start again.
  • 1 L is label 1, and 1 CASTEP ! then runs one generation.
\ block 1, run by pulser 1 on every birth at the watched cell
CAROW @ 7 AND 13 COLOUR C3 + PITCH !
CACOUNT @ 10 SHL FMAMT !
1 GATE !
  • CAROW @ 7 AND keeps the low three bits of the row: a number from 0 to 7. 13 COLOUR C3 + turns it into a pentatonic note.
  • CACOUNT @ 10 SHL is the number of live cells times 1024: the more crowded the row, the more FM.
\ setup, run once: tap cell 3; a birth fires pulser 1
3 CATAP !  1 CATRIG !  30 CARULE !

Deep Loop

The patch is described in a tape-loop patch, step by step. Its three blocks are:

\ block 0: a low note, one time in three
3 RND 0 =  1 JZ
  5 RND 13 COLOUR  C2 8 ST + +  PITCH !
  1 GATE !
1 L
  • 3 RND 0 = is true one time in three (when the random number is 0). 1 JZ jumps to the end, doing nothing, the other two times in three. So this block plays rarely.
  • The note is a pentatonic note over C2, plus 8 ST: eight semitones, which lifts the root to A flat.
\ block 2: let the loop breathe, one time in four
4 RND 0 =  1 JZ
  16000 RND 6000 +  DLYIN !
1 L

This one picks a new input level for the delay, from 6000 to 21999, so the loop slowly swells and thins. Block 1 is the same as block 0 but one octave higher and one time in four.

12Word reference

Every word of the language, with its stack picture. The top of the stack is on the right: ( a b -- c ) means b was on top, and c is left in place of both. Numbers are 16 bit and signed, and a result that goes past the ends sticks there instead of wrapping (see Numbers stop at the ends; the bit words are the exception). Pitches are numbers too, 256 to a semitone: see Pitch.

DUP( a -- a a )

Copy the top number.

DROP( a -- )

Throw the top number away.

SWAP( a b -- b a )

Swap the top two numbers.

OVER( a b -- a b a )

Copy the second number to the top.

ROT( a b c -- b c a )

Bring the third number to the top.

+( a b -- a+b )

Add. A sum past 32767 stays at 32767, and one below -32768 stays there: numbers stick at the ends, they do not wrap.

-( a b -- a-b )

Subtract the top from the one below. Sticks at the ends of the range like +.

*( a b -- a*b )

Multiply whole numbers: 6 7 * leaves 42. Sticks at the ends of the range like + and -. To scale by a fraction use F*.

F*( a b -- a*b )

Multiply as fractions: 32768 counts as 1.0, so .5 .5 F* leaves .25 (8192). The way to scale a register by a fraction, or to turn one level down by another. 20000 .5 F* leaves 10000.

/( a b -- a/b )

Divide whole numbers, rounding towards zero. Dividing by zero leaves 0 and flags a fault.

*/( a b c -- a*b/c )

Multiply a by b and divide by c, keeping the full product in between, so nothing sticks until the final answer (unlike * followed by /). Use it for ratios: 100 3 4 */ leaves 75.

NEG( a -- -a )

Change the sign. -32768 has no positive twin, so it becomes 32767.

ABS( a -- |a| )

Drop the sign: the distance from zero. -32768 becomes 32767.

MIN( a b -- smaller )

The smaller of the two.

MAX( a b -- larger )

The larger of the two.

MOD( a b -- a mod b )

The remainder after dividing by b. For a positive b the answer is 0 up to b-1, even if a is negative. Good for counting round a loop.

AND( a b -- a&b )

Keep the bits set in both numbers. Use it to mask or test a bit.

OR( a b -- a|b )

Set every bit that is set in either.

XOR( a b -- a^b )

Set the bits that differ. XOR with a bit twice puts it back: a toggle.

NOT( a -- ~a )

Flip every one of the 16 bits.

SHL( a n -- a<<n )

Shift the bits left n places, which doubles the number n times (the same as multiplying by a power of two). The result sticks at the end of the range. Only the low four bits of n count.

SHR( a n -- a>>n )

Shift the 16 bits right n places and fill with zeros, so a negative number becomes a large positive one. Only the low four bits of n count.

ROL( a n -- rotated )

Rotate the 16 bits left n places: the bits that fall off the top come back in at the bottom, so none are lost. Slides a pattern round a ring, such as a rhythm mask (SQEN) or the automaton's row (CAROW). Only the low four bits of n count.

ROR( a n -- rotated )

Rotate the 16 bits right n places: the bits that fall off the bottom come back in at the top. The mirror of ROL.

=( a b -- flag )

1 if equal.

<( a b -- flag )

1 if a is less than b.

>( a b -- flag )

1 if a is greater than b.

U<( a b -- flag )

1 if a is less than b when both are read as unsigned 16-bit numbers (0 to 65535). For bit patterns.

@( addr -- value )

Read a register. A register's name is just its address, so CUTOFF @ reads the cutoff.

!( value addr -- )

Write a register: 12000 CUTOFF ! sets the cutoff. Registers keep their own limits (most hold 0 to 32767). Read-only registers and bad addresses flag a fault.

L( n -- )

Mark a place in the block as label n (0 to 15). Write the number and then L: 3 L. A jump to 3 lands just after it.

JMP( n -- )

Jump to label n.

JZ( flag n -- )

Jump to label n if the flag is 0.

JNZ( flag n -- )

Jump to label n if the flag is not 0.

SKIP( flag -- )

If the flag is 0, skip the next token. Every token is one slot (a number, a note name, a register name or a word), so what you skip is exactly what you see. 7 0 SKIP 5 NEG leaves -7: the 5 was skipped and the NEG still ran. To skip more than one token, jump to a label with JZ instead.

EXIT( -- )

Stop now. The block (or the word being run) ends here, with no fault.

YIELD( -- )

Stop here, and next time this block runs, carry on from this point instead of the top. The way to make a block step through a sequence. Not allowed inside a word.

TRIG( n -- )

Fire pulser n (0 to 3): the blocks that pulser is wired to run at the next tick.

ROUTE( src dst w -- )

Wire a modulation source to a register, with a weight: the same as a line in the MATRIX tab. A pair already wired just changes its weight.

W( n -- )

Run word n (0 to 15), a short program kept apart from the blocks (24 slots). It shares the stack. Not allowed inside a word.

RND( n -- r )

A random whole number from 0 up to n-1. Gives 0 if n is not above 0.

ST( n -- pitch )

Semitones to a pitch distance (n times 256). 7 ST is a fifth up; add it to a pitch to transpose.

HZ( t -- pitch )

A frequency in tenths of a hertz to a pitch: 4400 HZ is A4.

COLOUR( index col -- pitch )

A note of a five-note scale in just intonation (pure ratios, not equal temperament). index walks up the scale (5 notes an octave; negative goes below the root) and col, 0 to 15, picks the flavour: bits 2 and 3 choose the second note from four, bits 0 and 1 the top note from four. The answer is the distance above the root, so add the root yourself.

?( a b flag -- a or b )

Pick one: leaves b if the flag is not 0, and a if it is 0.

SCALE( index scale -- pitch )

A note of one of the quantiser's scales (0 chromatic, 1 major, 2 minor, 3 dorian, 4 major pentatonic, 5 minor pentatonic, 6 blues, 7 whole tone; other numbers wrap round, so 8 is 0 again). index is the step up the scale, counted from 0 at the root; it wraps into the next octave after the last note (negative goes below the root). The answer is the distance above the root, so add the root yourself.

P( percent -- flag )

Chance: 1 that many times in a hundred, otherwise 0. 50 P is a coin toss, 10 P is rare, 100 P always. The same as 100 RND percent <.
